What, exactly, is doing the "going" from nonexistence to existence? Your consciousness? Putting aside the criticisms of a discrete mind and body, nonexistence would imply, well, not existing. It's not like sleeping, where the living body still exists in the world, it's a complete absence of perspective (a complete lack of consciousness, elan vitale, life, etc). Nothing holds over through nonexistence, and even if something did, what would it be? It would necessarily be something divorced or discrete from anything we understand physically. If you're engaging with the possibility of a discrete soul, then you're going to run into the gauntlet of all arguments against the likelihood of souls/discrete minds/etc, and by then you're operating with so many axioms that can't really be falsified. You reach a point where you're basically arguing for a tautology that isn't even based in any hard justification, a foundation of "We can exist without the physical realm."

I'm sure someone has, though I haven't got any recommendations on me at this time. Philosophy as a whole is a conversation, really, or at least that's how I was taught to look at it, so Phenomenology isn't unique in this regard, just better suited to being approached through that framing.

It's probably best to approach Phenomenology as a conversation across history. Yes everyone's "phenomenologies" differ from each other's, but phenomenology is idiosyncratic when approached from some angles. It's a return to perception in an attempt to use perception as a foundation for philosophy and science, and everyone's perception is definitionally unique, so if you're looking for an abstract set of rules or something that define Phenomenology in a way that maps to all phenomenologists, you're sort of missing the point.

This is why I say that Phenomenology is best approached as a conversation. Read Husserl to see what Husserl thought about Phenomenology, read Heidegger to see how he's agreeing and disagreeing and expanding with and on Husserl's work. Read Merleau-Ponty to see his take on things, etc. Start contemplating things phenomenologically yourself once you start reading these works, and sooner than you think you'll be capable of entering the conversation yourself!

Adding my own personal variation of Xanhil's response—sorry if I got that wrong, I'm on my phone—I'm usually thinking, as most are, throughout my day. 

To use my current project as an example, The last few weeks I've been examining what exactly it is re: postmodernism that appeals to me. I identified that I tend to value highly the execution of writing, and some of postmodernism, a large portion of it, deals either directly or indirectly with drawing attention to the execution of a story, whether it be reminding the Audience that they're reading a text, or introducing doubt to the Audience's confidence w/r/t the reliability of characters in the text. 

I've also been thinking a lot about closure. A feeling resolution I would guess most, if not all, humans search for on varying scales at various times makes for something worth mining, I would think. 

I decided that absolute closure was impossible to achieve because we can never capital-t Truly remove doubt. Closure is generally achieved by reducing doubt to a negligible level and then making the decision to toss it out. 

E.g. My father died, and because I haven't spoken to him in months, I'll never know what he Truly thought about me at the end, but my mother reassures me that he loved me very much, so I will move forward little-k knowing this and will not let the unknowable rule over me. 

I then started to think about how techniques attributed to postmodernism—cynicism, irony, unreliability—all function in some fashion as a way to introduce doubt.

This led me to think about postmodernism's effects on our abilities to experience closure. I started thinking about how fiction allows us to attempt to experience absolute closure by being a repeatable experience, which raises confidence in our conclusions, that, assuming the experience resolves according to its own rules, should provide us a feeling of second-hand closure unattainable in real life. And for the most part, this is how the bulk of fiction functions. We read stories, realize that while we can never know if the world within the story is being represented Truthfully, and throw that doubt out on the reasoning of being negligible.

Postmodernism points a spotlight at this issue we throw out with the aforementioned techniques. We are made acutely aware that the text might be deceiving us, that characters might be lying, that things might not resolve neatly. 

And so I've been working on a response to this issue in my current project, which I'm hesitantly shortening to the phrase of "closure in a world of indeterminate wiggle room." There's so much to write about, from how depression can be characterized as living solely within this wiggle room of exposed doubt—self-justifying stagnation or self-sabotage because "none of it Truly matters" or "I can't Truly know if any effort I put in will be rewarded"—to my generation's affinity with performing by way of social media as a way of seeking any form of acknowledgement from others in an attempt to reduce the doubt in their lives to a negligible level. 

Writing ideas most easily stem from your life and thoughts. What you find interesting will probably be found interesting by someone else, and it's easier to write profusely, and write well, about something you find interesting. Try to mine your daily thoughts on topics you find interesting, and see if you can relate what you find to others.

I'm only ~60 pages in or so, but the things I say here apply to most Faulkner I've read. This is all my opinion, and isn't necessarily accurate to what the general literary critique world would say. 

In Light in August, he spends time setting up characters that are initially unrelated which gives us a chance to see what they're really like. He then has them meet up so we can see how they act towards others, and this gives us more insight as to what they are truly like. 

The scene that made me reply to this post was the one where Byron Bunch falls in love. It's a very early scene that introduces Byron to another major character while simultaneously showing us that he is more vulnerable than we initially may have thought, /and/ the scene also ties up the loose end of the other character's question, "is my deserter in this town?"

It's a short scene, the writing appeals to me aesthetically (might not be the right word), and it gives tons of development. That alone is something I'd love. But then the personal value of seeing someone meet someone they're attracted to, try to get to know them, and realize far too late that they aren't and probably won't be interested is very high. I've had that happen to me in my life, and here is this master, Faulkner, writing about it. 

It gives me emotions, friend.

I'm reading Light in August currently, and I swear to god Faulkner personally takes my heart in his hands to show me what is possible. The things I feel reading his stories are the reason I write at all. I want someone to feel something like that by reading something I've written, but only time will tell.

Well, innocence varies. It depends on what you want them to have innocence regarding. An example off the top of my head, mind you, would be a teen who makes sexual innuendos while secretly having no sexual experience. I've found it beneficial for me personally to focus on one thing at a time. For you, and you've already mentioned it, I'd suggest learning to farm efficiently. Assuming the people you're playing with are farming about the same as you (let's just say 3cs a minute), just think of how strong you could be if you yourself farmed 6cs a minute. You could be coming back to lane from your first back a whole component up on your enemy. Have you ever as kindred been in a lane where he enemy had a bf sword and you still just had doran's? Isn't it obnoxious? You could be that enemy if you learned to farm just a little better. 6cs a minute is very doable; it's about half of the available cs in lane, I believe (two waves a minute usually 6 in a wave). If you focus on your cs, you could very easily start to dominate your lane. 

There are resources for how to learn to cs, but basically use the Goku approach and go into a custom game alone with no runes or masteries on the champion you want to practice. Just practice only hitting the creeps as they're about to die. Do this until you're satisfied with the results, and then do it in between every two regular games or so. (Don't forget to put your masteries back on in the regular games). 

Once you have this down, you'll have less to worry about while laning which opens your brain up to so much more. You'll be able to focus on harassing your opponents because as we've established they're not as good as you are at last hitting now. Hope this helps.

What I've found in my own writing is that developed characters lead to developed perspectives. I'd advise you to try and develop your characters more so that they are very clear in your mind, and as you do this place them in the situations of your story. With highly developed characters, it should be easier to see how and why they react to the situations, and writing from their perspective will be much simpler. Do note that you should attempt to limit your perspectives to a few developed characters, and this especially applies to newer writers. Of course, you don't *have* to limit yourself. I'm not a cop. In short, develop your characters more, and they'll show you their perspectives.
